Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Nisha Patel is a 22-year-old South Asian American woman who came to treatment after months of trying to push away what happened to her on the job. She is single and had been working as a delivery driver, spending most days alone in her car, moving between apartment complexes, gas stations, and front porches. The robbery happened during an evening delivery. She had parked, stepped out with an order, and was approached before she had time to make sense of what was happening. A man closed the distance quickly, directing her where to stand and what to hand over. What stayed with her was not only the theft itself but the feeling of being overtaken by someone else’s commands, her body complying while her mind lagged behind. She remembered a few sharp, frozen moments rather than a full sequence: the man’s position near her car, the way he controlled where she moved, and the sound of his voice telling her what to do. Later, when memories came back, they often arrived as those isolated visual snapshots, accompanied by the voice she had heard that night, as if the command were sounding again in her head.

In the days afterward, Nisha told herself it had not really happened the way she thought, or that maybe it was not that bad. She found herself repeating this when other people asked how she was doing, and even when she was alone. At other times the event did not come back as a clear picture at all. Instead, she would suddenly feel the same surge of fear and helplessness in her body, with no full image attached, and be left trying to understand why her heart was racing. She had also come to believe that she should have done more in the moment. Even though she had been frightened and compliant, she judged herself harshly for not stopping it, not resisting, not somehow changing the outcome. Alongside that guilt was a broader conviction that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. The robbery had left her feeling that safety could disappear instantly and that her own actions might not matter.

Returning to delivery work became difficult in ways that felt painfully specific. Being in a vehicle, whether driving herself or riding with someone else, became something she increasingly avoided. The car was too closely tied to the robbery scene and to the vulnerable feeling of arriving somewhere alone. She would delay shifts, cancel plans that required rides, and make excuses to others rather than admit how frightened she felt. When she did have to go somewhere, she scanned constantly for people she considered suspicious: someone lingering too long near an entrance, someone watching her, someone moving toward her in a way she could not predict. She could not settle in any place until she had identified how she would get out. In stores, apartment hallways, and pickup locations, her attention went first to doors, stairwells, and gaps between people. Even at home she found herself waking in the night to check that she was safe before she could attempt sleep again.

Certain encounters were especially difficult because they echoed the original loss of control. Any situation in which someone seemed to be ordering her around or forcing her into compliance could provoke an immediate internal jolt. She noticed this with customers giving abrupt instructions, with strangers crowding her space, and particularly around police. The sight of police officers was enough to make her body tense and her mind race, and she struggled to explain why except that authority itself now felt loaded and dangerous. She was also unable to relax even when she knew, logically, that she was in a safe place. Friends would tell her to calm down, but calm did not feel available to her body anymore.

Over the following months her world narrowed. She used drugs at times to blunt the intensity of what she felt and to get temporary distance from the fear, the wakefulness, and the sudden return of the man’s voice in her mind. At the same time, she felt increasingly cut off from other people. Being 22, she watched peers move easily through ordinary routines—driving, going out, laughing off small risks—while she felt separate from them, as if she now lived by different rules. The concrete cost showed up in her work: avoiding driving threatened her ability to keep doing deliveries, and the job that had structured her days became another source of dread.

By the time she sought help, what finally pushed her to come in was the sense that she was organizing her whole life around danger and still never feeling safe. She was exhausted from waking to check on her surroundings, from constantly locating exits, and from trying to deny an event that kept returning in pieces and sounds. What frightened her most was the belief that this was now who she was—someone unable to protect herself, someone set apart from everyone else. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to feel less controlled by the robbery and less trapped by the expectation that bad things could happen at any moment.
